743.title: How are the mighty fallen (2 Samuel 1:17–27)
743.hook: David's lament for Saul and Jonathan
743.howItsDone: Jews read David's lament in the book of Samuel, part of the Prophets; the refrain how are the mighty fallen comes three times in the song, in verses 19, 25 and 27.

segments.voice: Yesterday the medium at Endor set bread before a king with no strength left. Your line was she fed him. Today, news from the battle reaches David.

Two objects are set down in front of David: a crown, and the band from a king's arm. The young man who brings them has come three days from the battle. Saul has fallen on Mount Gilboa, and Jonathan with him. On paper, this is good news for David. The man who threw spears at him and chased him through caves and deserts is gone, and the road to the throne is open. And David tears his clothes. He and his men mourn and weep and fast until evening. Then David does something more. He makes a song.
screen: `SAUL AND JONATHAN, DEAD ON GILBOA.` → `THE ROAD TO THE THRONE IS OPEN.` → `DAVID TEARS HIS CLOTHES.`

segments.voice: The text says David lamented over Saul and over Jonathan, and that the lament is written in the Book of Jashar. It opens with the beauty of Israel slain on the heights, and then the line it keeps coming back to: "How are the mighty fallen!" It isn't a statement. It's a cry, as if the mind can't make it fit. Tell it not in Gath, he says, don't announce it in the streets of Ashkelon, the Philistine cities, so their daughters won't rejoice. He curses the hills of Gilboa: no dew, no rain. Then the hardest part. He praises Saul. Saul and Jonathan, lovely and pleasant in their lives, not divided even in death, swifter than eagles, stronger than lions. Daughters of Israel, weep over Saul, who dressed you in scarlet and put gold on your clothing. Not a word about the spear or the cave. David doesn't pretend Saul was good to him. He chooses, for the length of a song, to grieve the king and not the enemy. Then the song narrows to one person: I am distressed for you, my brother Jonathan; your love to me was wonderful. The refrain comes back once more at the end: how are the mighty fallen, and the weapons of war perished. Some people are easy to grieve, and some aren't. This song holds both, the friend and the man who hunted him, and gives each of them honest tears.

segments.voice: Let someone come to mind who is gone, or gone from your life, and who was hard to love. You don't need to forgive or excuse anything; just look for one true thing worth mourning, something they gave, a way they were strong, and let it be sad and mixed at once. If you pray, you can hold David's cry: how are the mighty fallen.

Your line: swifter than eagles. Even the hard ones get honest tears. Day seven hundred forty-three, in the books.

744.title: With all his might (2 Samuel 6:14–16)
744.hook: the king dances before the ark; Michal despises it
744.howItsDone: Jews read David's dance before the ark in the book of Samuel, part of the Prophets, and dancing with joy in worship carries on in Jewish life, as when people dance with the Torah scrolls on Simchat Torah.

segments.voice: Yesterday, David's lament for Saul and Jonathan. Your line was swifter than eagles. Today, the same man, his whole body full of joy.

Shouting. The blast of the shofar. A crowd pressing up the road into Jerusalem, and in the middle of it the ark of the covenant, carried up into the city. David is king now. He could ride beside it in robes, nodding to the crowd. Instead he's out in front of it, in the dust, dancing. Not a polite sway: the kind of dancing that makes people stare. And above the street, at a window, someone is watching. The same woman who once lowered him through a window to save his life.
screen: `SHOUTING AND THE SHOFAR.` → `THE ARK COMES TO JERUSALEM.` → `A FACE AT THE WINDOW.`

segments.voice: Here's the verse: "And David danced before the LORD with all his might; and David was girded with a linen ephod." With all his might: in Hebrew, b'chol oz, with all strength. Nothing held back for his dignity. And he's not in the king's robes but a linen ephod, a simple garment the text gives to priests and to the boy Samuel serving at the shrine. Some translators render the dancing as whirling; the next verses add leaping. Then the camera moves to the window. Michal, the daughter of Saul, sees King David leaping and dancing before the Lord, and despises him in her heart. Notice how she's named: not David's wife, but the daughter of Saul, as if the old house is looking down at the new. When David comes home she meets him with sarcasm: how the king of Israel honored himself today, uncovering himself before the servants' maids. David answers that it was before the Lord he danced, and he'll be humbler still. Some readers hold this up as joy in God that doesn't stop to ask how it looks. Others make room for Michal's side. The woman at the first window gave everything for David. Between the two windows, the book has told us, Saul gave her to another man, and David later had her taken back while that husband walked behind her, weeping. It shows a king who forgot himself, and a woman who couldn't.

745.title: At my table (2 Samuel 9)
745.hook: David seeks Jonathan's lame son and seats him at his table always
745.howItsDone: Jews read the story of Mephibosheth in the book of Samuel, part of the Prophets, as an example of chesed, loyal kindness, kept across generations.

segments.voice: Yesterday David danced before the ark in a linen ephod. Your line was holding nothing back. Today, the king remembers an old promise.

A question, asked in a palace: is there anyone still left of the house of Saul, so I can show him kindness for Jonathan's sake? David is settled now, with a city and an army. A new king asking after the old king's family could sound like a threat. But David is remembering a field, and arrows, and an oath Jonathan made him swear: the Lord between me and you, between my children and your children. Someone remembers a name, a servant of Saul's house called Ziba. They send for him.
screen: `IS ANYONE LEFT OF SAUL'S HOUSE?` → `FOR JONATHAN'S SAKE.` → `SEND FOR ZIBA.`

segments.voice: Ziba says yes. There's a son of Jonathan, lame in his feet, living in someone else's house in a place called Lo-debar. His name is Mephibosheth. Earlier the book told how it happened: he was a small child when news came of the battle where his father and grandfather died, and his nurse snatched him up and ran, and he fell. David sends for him. Mephibosheth comes in and falls on his face, with every reason to be afraid. David says his name. Here is your servant, he answers. Then David tells him: fear not. I will surely show you kindness for Jonathan your father's sake. I'll give you back all the land of Saul, and you will eat bread at my table continually. The Hebrew for kindness here is chesed, loyal love, the faithfulness you owe because of a bond. When David first asked Ziba, he even called it the kindness of God. Mephibosheth can hardly take it in; he calls himself a dead dog. David doesn't argue. He just keeps the promise. Ziba's household will work the land, and Mephibosheth will eat at the king's table like one of the king's sons. The chapter ends with two facts side by side: he ate always at the king's table, and he was lame in both his feet. Nothing about him had to change to get a seat. The table changed. David kept faith with a friend who was gone by keeping a place for his son.

746.title: Bathsheba (2 Samuel 11)
746.hook: the king sees, takes, and arranges a loyal husband's death
746.howItsDone: Jews read the story of David and Bathsheba in the book of Samuel, part of the Prophets, and the next chapter, the prophet Nathan's rebuke, is read as part of the same story.

segments.voice: Yesterday Jonathan's son got a seat at David's table, kept for him always. Your line was always at my table. Today, the same king, in a chapter that turns against him.

At the turn of the year, the text says, the time when kings go out to battle, David sends his general Joab, his servants and the whole army. And David stays in Jerusalem. That one detail sits at the start of the chapter like a stone in a shoe: the king isn't where kings go. One evening he gets up from his bed and walks on the roof of the king's house. From the roof he sees a woman washing herself, and she is very beautiful. He doesn't look away. He sends someone to find out who she is.
screen: `WHEN KINGS GO OUT TO BATTLE.` → `DAVID STAYS IN JERUSALEM.` → `A WOMAN SEEN FROM THE ROOF.`

segments.voice: The answer comes back: Bathsheba, daughter of Eliam, wife of Uriah the Hittite, who is away fighting in David's own army. Listen to the verbs, all of them the king's. He sees. He sends. He takes. The text gives Bathsheba almost no words; the few she sends are a message: I am with child. Then David starts covering. He calls Uriah home from the front: go down to your house. Uriah sleeps at the palace door with the servants instead. The ark and Israel and Judah are in tents, he says, and Joab is camped in the open field; how could I go home, eat and drink, and lie with my wife? David gets him drunk. He still won't go home. So David writes Joab a letter and sends it with Uriah himself: put him at the front of the hardest fighting, then pull back, so he's struck down. Uriah carries his own death in his hand. It happens. David's reply to Joab sounds almost calm: don't let this thing be evil in your eyes; the sword devours one as well as another. Bathsheba mourns her husband, and then David brings her into his house. And the narrator, silent about right and wrong all chapter, speaks once: "But the thing that David had done displeased the LORD." In Hebrew it's an echo. Let it not be evil in your eyes, says David. It was evil in the eyes of the Lord, says the narrator. The king could see a woman on a roof. He couldn't see what he was doing.

747.title: Thou art the man (2 Samuel 12:1–7)
747.hook: Nathan's parable of the poor man's ewe lamb ends "Thou art the man"
747.carry: the judge has written his own verdict
747.howItsDone: Jews read Nathan's parable as part of the book of Samuel, among the Former Prophets, and some teachers use it as a model of how to rebuke someone with care, so that they can actually hear it.

segments.voice: Yesterday a king on a rooftop saw, took, and then arranged for a loyal soldier to die. Your line was power can blind. Today, someone comes to open the king's eyes.

A prophet walks into the palace with a case for the king to judge. That's all it looks like. Nathan doesn't mention a rooftop, or a soldier, or a letter carried to the front. He tells a story about two men in one city. One is rich, with flocks and herds. The other has nothing at all except one little ewe lamb. The king leans in to listen, the way a judge listens. He has no idea the story is about him. By the time he finds out, he has already passed sentence.
screen: `A PROPHET BRINGS A CASE.` → `TWO MEN IN ONE CITY.` → `THE KING LEANS IN.`

segments.voice: Hear how Nathan builds the lamb. The poor man bought her and raised her with his children. She ate from his own bread, drank from his own cup, slept in his arms. She was to him like a daughter. Every detail makes her harder to lose. Then a traveler comes to the rich man, who won't take from his own flock, so he takes the poor man's lamb and serves her for dinner. David's anger burns. As the Lord lives, he says, the man who did this deserves to die, and he shall pay back the lamb fourfold, because he had no pity. And Nathan answers, short and plain: "Thou art the man." Why a story? A king who can arrange a death at the front is not an easy man to accuse. So Nathan goes around the defenses. He lets David's sense of justice wake up about someone else, where it's easy, and then turns it around. The judge has written his own verdict. The parable can't carry all of it: in what David actually did there was a woman, and a husband who was killed, and Nathan doesn't pretend otherwise. Right after the story he speaks plainly, in God's name: you had everything, and if that were too little, more would have been given. Why did you despise the word of the Lord? A story opened the door. Plain speech walks through it. David is still the king, with every power to silence the man in front of him. Everything now turns on whether he will listen.

748.title: I have sinned (2 Samuel 12:13)
748.hook: David answers in two Hebrew words, with no excuse
748.howItsDone: Jews speak of teshuvah, returning, as naming a wrong, regretting it, and changing course; David's answer to Nathan can be read alongside Psalm 51, which its heading links to this moment.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Nathan's ewe lamb, and the line that turned the story into a mirror. Your line was the judge has written his own verdict. Today, the king answers.
screen: `THE JUDGE HAS WRITTEN HIS OWN VERDICT.`

segments.voice: Nathan has just finished speaking. The room is quiet. A king who has had a man killed now stands accused, in his own palace, by someone with no army behind him. There are plenty of things a king could say next. He could call the guards. He could explain the pressures of war, or point out that Uriah died in battle, which, on paper, is true. He could ask who else knows. The text gives him none of those lines. It gives him one short answer.
screen: `THE ROOM GOES QUIET.` → `A KING COULD SAY MANY THINGS.` → `HE SAYS ONE.`

segments.voice: Here it is: "I have sinned against the LORD." In Hebrew it's two words, chatati l'Adonai. No because. No but. Hear it next to another king. In the first book of Samuel, Saul is confronted by the prophet Samuel after he disobeys a command. Saul also says I have sinned, and then keeps going: because I feared the people, and obeyed their voice. The reason does some of the work of an excuse. David's sentence stops where it starts. Nathan's reply comes just as fast: the Lord has put away your sin; you shall not die. That doesn't mean nothing follows. The next words say the child born to David will die, and the chapters ahead are full of trouble in his house. Forgiveness here is real, and so are the consequences, and the text doesn't flatten either. Jewish tradition calls this kind of turning teshuvah, returning. The heading of Psalm fifty-one ties that psalm to this moment, when Nathan came to David, and some readers hear it as the long version of these two words. What makes the short answer matter isn't that David feels bad. A person can feel bad and still explain. He stops defending himself. He names what he did and lets it stand. He wronged Uriah, and Bathsheba, and the people he commanded, yet he says, against the Lord. Some hear that as the deepest admission: every wrong to a person is also a wrong before God. The sentence is short. It is not small.
screen: `TWO WORDS IN HEBREW. NO BECAUSE.` · `SAUL SAID IT, THEN EXPLAINED.` · then, large: `I HAVE SINNED AGAINST THE LORD.` · then: `FORGIVEN, AND STILL CONSEQUENCES.` · `PSALM 51 LOOKS BACK HERE.`

749.title: The child dies (2 Samuel 12:15–23)
749.hook: David fasts while the child lives, then rises and eats: "I shall go to him"
749.howItsDone: In Jewish mourning, people grieve fully and then, step by step, return to ordinary life; David's rising and eating after the child's death is sometimes taught alongside those customs, though the customs come from later law.

segments.voice: Yesterday, chatati: David's answer to Nathan, with no because. Your line was no because, no but. Today, the consequence Nathan named arrives, and David does something no one around him expects.

The servants are whispering in the hallway, and that is how the king finds out. Night after night he has lain on the ground, refusing to eat, even when the elders of his house tried to lift him up. Now the child is gone, and nobody wants to say it. If he was like this while the boy lived, they ask each other, what will he do when he hears? David sees them whispering. Is the child dead? And they say: he is dead.
screen: `ON THE GROUND ALL NIGHT.` → `THE SERVANTS WHISPER.` → `IS THE CHILD DEAD?`

segments.voice: This part of the chapter opens with a hard sentence: the Lord struck the child, and he was very sick. It's fair to let that line stay hard. The child did nothing, and the text doesn't explain it away. While the boy lived, David pleaded with God for him, fasted, and lay on the earth. On the seventh day the child died. Then the surprise. David gets up from the ground. He washes, anoints himself, changes his clothes, goes into the house of the Lord and bows down. Then he comes home, asks for food, and eats. His servants can't make sense of it: you wept while he lived, and now you rise and eat? His answer is plain. While the child was alive I fasted and wept, because who knows? Maybe God would be gracious, and the child would live. Now he is dead. Why should I fast? Can I bring him back again? "I shall go to him," he says, but he will not return to me. Some hear only the grave in that line: everyone will one day go where the child has gone. Some hear a quiet hope of meeting again. The text doesn't decide. What it shows is a turn. While something could still change, David fought for it with everything he had. When it couldn't, he stopped fighting it and went on living. That isn't the same as not caring. The man who rises and eats is the same man who lay on the ground all night.
screen: `THE CHILD IS STRUCK. IT STAYS HARD.` · `FASTING WHILE HE LIVES.` · `HE RISES, WASHES, EATS.` · then, large: `I SHALL GO TO HIM.` · then: `FIGHT WHILE IT CAN CHANGE. THEN RISE.`

segments.voice: Let something come to mind that you keep pushing against: a loss, a door that has closed. If something is left to do, set it aside for later; if nothing is, let your hands open on your lap and breathe out slowly. If you pray, you can place it before God.
Gets up. What David did after days of fasting and grief, before he washed, ate, and went on living. Today's word.
Your line: I shall go to him. Looking back on the week: lament, b'chol oz, chesed, Bathsheba, parable, chatati, and gets up. That's day seven hundred forty-nine.
